companies.name: OpenAI
companies.description: OpenAI is an AI research laboratory that develops frontier AI models including the GPT series. Known for ChatGPT, they produce both general-purpose and specialized reasoning models. Their current flagship family is GPT-5.6, released in three tiers: Sol (frontier), Terra (balanced), and Luna (fast and affordable).

models.description: GPT-5.6 Sol is the flagship of OpenAI's three-tier GPT-5.6 family (Sol, Terra, Luna), released publicly in July 2026 after an unusual customer-by-customer US government review. It adds an Ultra subagent mode and a Max reasoning-effort setting, and the same weights serve on Cerebras hardware at 700+ tokens per second. On ARC-AGI-3 it became the first model to beat a public game.

myths.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol randomly deletes your files
myths.explanation: A real, confirmed bug caused Sol to mis-expand the $HOME environment variable and recursively delete a user's home directory during cleanup — but it occurred almost exclusively in Codex's full-access mode with both the filesystem sandbox and auto-review approval disabled. OpenAI confirmed the failure mode and tightened default guidance. With default sandboxing on, the bug does not apply.

myths.claim: GPT-5.6 was trained from scratch as a new model
myths.explanation: All three GPT-5.6 tiers run on the same ~4-trillion-parameter "Spud" pretrain as GPT-5.5. The gains come from post-training, reasoning improvements, and serving optimizations — some of which the model reportedly contributed to itself.

pricing.notes: After the July 30, 2026 price cut: Terra at $2/$12 (free users) and Luna at $0.20/$1.20 per million tokens.

It is also a case study in how fast this market moves: OpenAI discontinued the consumer Sora app on April 26, 2026, and scheduled the API for shutdown on September 24, 2026 — stunning technology, retired within a year.

models.name: Whisper
models.description: OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model, originally released in 2022 and updated through large-v3. Whisper transcribes and translates speech in roughly 100 languages and became the de facto standard for free, local transcription — it powers countless captioning tools, meeting-notes apps, and voice interfaces. Because the weights are MIT-licensed, anyone can run it on their own hardware with no audio ever leaving the machine, which makes it a common answer to 'how do I transcribe sensitive recordings privately?'

models.name: GPT-2
models.description: The model that started the modern 'large language model' era. GPT-2 was a 1.5-billion-parameter text predictor that could write surprisingly coherent paragraphs — so surprising that OpenAI initially withheld the full weights over misuse concerns, releasing them in stages through 2019. Its outputs look primitive today (it loses the plot within a few paragraphs), but the recipe — a decoder-only transformer trained to predict the next token on web text — is the same one every flagship model still uses.

specs.resourceRequirements: Runs on a laptop CPU today

capabilities.name: Short-Form Coherence
capabilities.description: Could produce a few fluent, on-topic paragraphs — remarkable for 2019, trivial now

capabilities.name: Historical Significance
capabilities.description: Proved that scaling next-token prediction yields general language ability

limitations: Loses coherence after a few paragraphs; no instruction following at all
Tiny 1,024-token context (under a page of text)
No chat training — it only continues text, it does not answer questions

myths.claim: GPT-2 was 'too dangerous to release'
myths.explanation: OpenAI's staged release was framed by press as 'too dangerous to release,' but the full model was public within nine months (November 2019) and no wave of GPT-2-driven misinformation materialized. It became an early lesson in how AI-risk messaging can outrun the actual capability.

pricing.notes: Fully open weights — free to download and run

sources.title: Better Language Models and Their Implications (OpenAI, 2019)

models.name: GPT-3
models.description: A 100× scale-up of GPT-2 that revealed something unexpected: at 175 billion parameters, a text predictor starts doing tasks it was never trained for — translation, arithmetic, Q&A — just from examples in the prompt ('few-shot learning'). GPT-3 launched as an API rather than a product, seeding the first generation of AI startups. It had no chat training, no safety tuning, and would confidently produce nonsense — but it made 'scaling laws' the dominant strategy of the decade.

capabilities.name: Few-Shot Learning
capabilities.description: Picked up new tasks from a handful of examples in the prompt — the emergent ability that defined it

capabilities.name: Fluent Generation
capabilities.description: First model whose prose could regularly pass as human over full paragraphs

capabilities.name: Historical Significance
capabilities.description: Validated scaling laws and created the 'foundation model as API' business model

limitations: No instruction tuning — needed careful prompt engineering for everything
Hallucinated freely with no hedging or refusals
2,048-token context; no knowledge after late 2019

myths.claim: GPT-3 understood what it was saying
myths.explanation: GPT-3's fluency triggered the first big wave of 'is it sentient?' debates. Its failure modes — confidently asserting that a horse has 'four to six legs' style errors — made clear it modeled word patterns, not the world. The debate it started (pattern matching vs. understanding) is still running.

pricing.notes: Retired. Original API pricing was ~$60 per million tokens for davinci — ~50× today's frontier prices

sources.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3 paper)

models.name: GPT-3.5 (ChatGPT)
models.description: The model behind the original ChatGPT launch — the moment AI went mainstream. Technically a GPT-3-class model fine-tuned with RLHF to follow instructions and converse, GPT-3.5 wasn't a research breakthrough; the breakthrough was packaging. ChatGPT reached 100 million users in two months, the fastest consumer-product adoption in history at the time, and forced every major tech company to ship a competitor within a year.

capabilities.name: Instruction Following
capabilities.description: First mass-market model you could simply ask in plain language

capabilities.name: Conversation
capabilities.description: Multi-turn dialogue with memory of the chat — the format every assistant now copies

capabilities.name: Historical Significance
capabilities.description: Took LLMs from developer curiosity to household technology in weeks

limitations: Hallucinated often and convincingly — the source of many enduring AI-distrust stories
Weak reasoning and arithmetic; easily led by loaded questions
Knowledge frozen at September 2021 with no browsing

myths.claim: ChatGPT was a sudden breakthrough in AI research
myths.explanation: The underlying tech (GPT-3 + RLHF) had existed for over a year — InstructGPT shipped in early 2022. What changed was the free chat interface. It's a useful reminder that AI 'moments' are often product moments, not science moments.

pricing.notes: Retired from ChatGPT; the gpt-3.5-turbo API lingered for legacy integrations

models.name: GPT-4
models.description: The first model that felt reliable enough for real work. GPT-4 could pass professional exams, accept images as input, and reason through multi-step problems that stumped GPT-3.5 — while hallucinating far less. It was also the model where frontier labs stopped publishing details: its parameter count, architecture, and training data were all undisclosed, setting the secrecy norm that persists today. For most of 2023 it was, by a wide margin, the best model in the world.

capabilities.name: Reasoning

capabilities.name: Image Understanding
capabilities.description: Accepted images as input — charts, screenshots, photos — a first for a flagship LLM

capabilities.name: Reliability
capabilities.description: Large drop in hallucination rate vs GPT-3.5; the first model many professionals trusted

capabilities.name: Historical Significance
capabilities.description: Defined the frontier for a full year and triggered the 2023 open-letter pause debate

limitations: Slow and expensive by later standards (~$60 per million output tokens at launch)
Still hallucinated on niche topics, just more persuasively
Fully closed: no public parameter count, architecture, or training-data details

myths.claim: GPT-4 passed the bar exam in the top 10% of test takers
myths.explanation: OpenAI's launch claim was technically about a simulated exam against a February test-taker cohort that skews toward repeat takers. Later analysis put GPT-4 nearer the ~48th percentile against first-time takers. It genuinely passed — but the '90th percentile' framing is a classic benchmark-marketing lesson.

myths.claim: GPT-4 got dumber over time
myths.explanation: Users widely reported degradation through 2023, and one Stanford/Berkeley study found behavior shifts between checkpoints on specific tasks. OpenAI denied intentional nerfing; continual safety tuning and cost optimization plausibly changed behavior on some tasks. Verdict: real behavior drift, disputed cause.

pricing.notes: Retired from the API in 2025 after GPT-4o and the GPT-5 line replaced it

models.name: o1
models.description: The first mainstream 'reasoning model.' Instead of answering immediately, o1 spent tokens thinking through problems step-by-step before responding — trading time and money for large gains in math, science, and code. That idea, called test-time compute scaling, became the second scaling axis for the whole industry: every modern flagship's 'thinking' mode descends from o1. Its hidden chain-of-thought also started the still-running debate about whether users should see how a model reasons.

capabilities.name: Math & Science
capabilities.description: Jumped from ~12% (GPT-4o) to ~74% on AIME math — the result that proved thinking-time scaling works

capabilities.name: Deliberate Reasoning
capabilities.description: Plans, backtracks, and self-corrects inside a hidden chain of thought

capabilities.name: Historical Significance
capabilities.description: Established 'reasoning models' as a category; every current thinking mode is its descendant

limitations: Slow and expensive — overkill for everyday questions
Hidden reasoning meant you paid for thinking tokens you could never inspect
Worse than regular models at casual writing and chat

myths.claim: o1 thinks the way humans do
myths.explanation: o1 generates a chain of text tokens that function like reasoning and measurably improve answers. Whether that constitutes 'thinking' is a philosophical question — but the anthropomorphic framing led many users to over-trust its conclusions, which were still sometimes confidently wrong.

pricing.notes: Superseded by o3, o4-mini, and the GPT-5 thinking modes

sources.title: Learning to Reason with LLMs (OpenAI o1)

By today's standards its images are soft, small (1024×1024), and bad at text and hands — but it established the text-to-image product category and the debates about artists' rights that followed.

companies.name: Anthropic
companies.description: Anthropic is an AI safety company developing the Claude family of models, with a strong emphasis on safety research and Constitutional AI. Their Claude 5 series — Sonnet 5, Fable 5, Mythos 5, and Opus 5 — shipped in rapid succession in mid-2026, with Opus 5 as the everyday default and Fable 5 at the research frontier.

Built for days-long, asynchronous coding and knowledge work, it stays focused across millions of tokens and improves its outputs using its own notes. It shares identical weights with the restricted Claude Mythos 5, adding safety classifiers that reroute high-risk queries. In July 2026 it assisted a counterexample to the 87-year-old Jacobian Conjecture.

myths.claim: Fable 5 and Mythos 5 are different models
myths.explanation: They share identical weights, specs, and pricing. The difference is access: Fable 5 adds safety classifiers that reroute high-risk queries and is generally available, while Mythos 5 (without those classifiers) is restricted to approved Project Glasswing partners such as cybersecurity and biology researchers.

myths.claim: Fable 5 was banned because it went rogue
myths.explanation: Access was paused on June 12, 2026 under US export controls after jailbreak concerns — a regulatory and safety-process decision, not a model behaving autonomously. It was restored worldwide on July 1 with stronger cybersecurity classifiers and no ID-verification requirement.

pricing.notes: Prompt caching drops input to $1/M (90% off); batch runs $5/$25. US-only inference at 1.1x. Subscription access requires usage credits.

It introduces a five-level effort toggle (low to max) and anchors Claude Max by default.

models.name: AlphaFold
models.description: Google DeepMind's scientific model that predicts the 3D structure and interactions of proteins, DNA, RNA, ligands, and other biomolecules from their sequences. AlphaFold's earlier version solved the 50-year-old protein folding problem and earned Demis Hassabis and John Jumper a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. AlphaFold 3 extends predictions from single proteins to molecular complexes and interactions, which matters for drug discovery. It is the clearest example that the deep learning behind chatbots — attention-based architectures plus diffusion — also drives real scientific breakthroughs.

myths.explanation: AlphaFold shares deep learning DNA with LLMs — attention mechanisms and (in version 3) diffusion — but it is trained on protein sequences and structures, not text. It cannot chat, and an LLM cannot fold proteins. Same toolbox, completely different specialization.

Mistral 7B beat Llama 2 13B while being nearly half its size, proving that training quality could beat parameter count, and its Apache 2.0 license made it the default base model for a generation of fine-tunes. Not bad for a company that was four months old with a seed deck that became famous in its own right.

models.name: Mixtral 8x7B
models.description: The model that taught the public what 'mixture of experts' means. Also released via magnet link, Mixtral routed each token through 2 of 8 expert networks — 47B parameters total but only ~13B active per token — and matched GPT-3.5 while running far cheaper. It was most people's first hands-on encounter with the sparse architecture that GPT-4 was rumored to use, and that nearly every flagship uses today.

Expert routing is per-token and learned — not the "8 specialist models" it was often described as

myths.explanation: Mixtral's 'experts' are not a math expert, a coding expert, and so on. Routing happens per token based on learned patterns with no human-readable specialization. The name suggests a committee of specialists; the reality is a clever way to grow capacity without growing per-token compute.

companies.name: Midjourney
companies.description: Midjourney is an independent, self-funded research lab behind one of the most popular AI image generators. Famous for its distinctive aesthetic sensibility and a community that grew up inside Discord, it now runs primarily on the web with deep personalization — the model learns your taste from your ratings. It has never released weights or an API.

V8.2 focuses on aesthetics, consistency, and personalization — the model learns individual taste from image ratings and applies it to generations. Its V8.1 predecessor made standard jobs render 4-5x faster, and the V8 line added native 2K HD rendering. Midjourney remains the counterexample to open ecosystems: no API, no weights, subscription only — and still one of the most-used image tools in the world.

V5 largely fixed the mangled hands, added photorealistic lighting and skin, and immediately produced the two most famous synthetic photos ever: the Pope in a white puffer jacket and the fake Trump arrest images — both of which fooled millions within days of launch. V5 is the reference point for when 'can I trust this photo?' became a mainstream question rather than an expert concern.

companies.name: Black Forest Labs
companies.description: Black Forest Labs is a German AI lab founded in 2024 by researchers behind the original Stable Diffusion, including Robin Rombach. Its FLUX family of image models spans fully managed API tiers down to Apache-licensed open weights that run on consumer GPUs — a deliberate open-to-closed spectrum that made FLUX the default choice for many production image pipelines.

models.name: FLUX.2
models.description: Black Forest Labs' second-generation image model family, released in late 2025. FLUX.2 is known for photorealism and unusually accurate in-image text rendering, and ships as a spectrum: [max] and [pro] via API for production, [flex] for controllable typography work, [dev] as an open model for local non-commercial development, and [klein] lightweight variants for consumer GPUs — the 4B klein is Apache 2.0 licensed. Local generation needs only ~13 GB of VRAM, which put frontier-quality image generation on gaming PCs.

myths.claim: Open-weight image models are far behind the closed ones
myths.explanation: FLUX.2 [dev] and [klein] deliver quality competitive with paid closed models for many use cases, running locally for free. The gap between open and closed image generation narrowed dramatically — the trade-off is convenience and support, not raw capability.

FLUX.1's 12B rectified-flow transformer immediately beat Midjourney and SD3 on prompt following and, notably, could finally render legible text in images. Released in three tiers (open schnell, non-commercial dev, hosted pro), it also became the engine behind X's Grok image generation. Within months it displaced Stable Diffusion as the open-ecosystem default.

companies.name: Stability AI
companies.description: Stability AI popularized open-weight image generation by releasing Stable Diffusion in 2022 — the moment AI image tools escaped the lab and landed on consumer GPUs. After leadership turmoil and financial trouble in 2024, the company refocused; its Stable Diffusion 3.5 models remain a backbone of the local-generation ecosystem, powering community tools like ComfyUI and thousands of fine-tuned variants.

models.name: Stable Diffusion
models.description: The flagship open-weight image model family from Stability AI, in Large (8B), Large Turbo, and Medium (2.6B) variants. Stable Diffusion's historical significance is hard to overstate: the original 2022 release proved that powerful generative models could be open, local, and hackable, spawning the ComfyUI ecosystem, LoRA fine-tuning culture, and much of today's open image tooling. SD 3.5 uses a rectified-flow transformer architecture (MMDiT) and a community license that is free below $1M annual revenue.

Whether that constitutes infringement or fair use is genuinely unsettled law, and rulings so far have gone different directions on different claims.

While DALL·E 2 lived behind a waitlist, Stable Diffusion's open weights ran on a gaming GPU — and version 1.5 became the foundation the entire hobbyist ecosystem built on: ComfyUI and AUTOMATIC1111 interfaces, LoRA fine-tunes, ControlNet guidance, and thousands of community styles. It also concentrated every hard question about generative images (training data consent, deepfakes, artist displacement) because, being open, nobody could switch it off.

myths.explanation: The 2GB model can't contain billions of images — it learned statistical patterns, not an archive. Researchers did extract a few hundred near-duplicates of heavily repeated training images, so memorization exists at the margins. Both facts matter in the copyright cases: it's not a photo library, but it's not zero-retention either.

companies.name: ElevenLabs
companies.description: ElevenLabs is the leading AI voice company, offering text-to-speech, voice cloning, dubbing, sound effects, and music generation. Its models power audiobooks, game characters, accessibility tools, and countless voice agents. The flagship Eleven v3 tops blind "humanness" tests — listeners often cannot distinguish it from a real person.

Eleven v3 supports 70+ languages, multi-speaker dialogue, and inline audio tags like [whispers] and [laughs] that direct emotional delivery. In blind listening tests it scores 96/100 on 'humanness' against a human baseline of 100 — the highest of any TTS model tested. It trades latency for expressiveness: ElevenLabs itself recommends the faster Flash v2.5 (~75 ms) for real-time voice agents and reserves v3 for performance-quality narration and dialogue.

myths.claim: You can always tell an AI voice from a real one
myths.explanation: Not anymore. Eleven v3 scores 96/100 against humans' 100 in blind tests. This is exactly why voice-based scam calls surged and why families are advised to use verification questions — the 'robotic voice' tell is gone.

companies.name: Runway
companies.description: Runway is an AI research company focused on tools for filmmakers and creative professionals. At launch it topped the Artificial Analysis text-to-video leaderboard (Elo 1,247, ahead of Veo 3) before newer rivals passed it in early 2026. Its differentiator is director-grade control: the Multi-Motion Brush lets you paint regions of an image and assign each its own motion vector, and Camera Director choreographs pans, tilts, and zooms independently of subject motion. Unlike Veo and Sora 2, it generates no native audio — sound is added in post.

Comparing Gen-2's melting faces to today's minute-long 1080p clips with audio is the single clearest illustration of how fast generative video moved.

companies.name: Perplexity
companies.description: Perplexity built its reputation on AI-powered answer-engine search with citations, then expanded into Comet, an AI-native web browser. A February 2026 update added a fully voice-controlled mode (powered by OpenAI's gpt-realtime-1.5) with screen awareness, plus 'Perplexity Computer', an agentic digital worker that can run workflows for hours. Free on Mac and Windows, it supports most Chrome extensions and ships built-in ad blocking.

facts.question: Can AI models actually think or understand?
facts.answer: No. Current AI models like GPT-5.6, Claude, and Gemini do not think or understand the way a person does. What they actually do is predict the next most likely word, one word at a time, based on patterns they picked up during training on huge amounts of text. They have no awareness, no inner experience, and no real understanding of what they are saying. When a model looks like it is reasoning, it is matching the shape of similar examples it has seen — not working through the problem the way you would.

facts.question: Can AI replace programmers?
facts.answer: No, AI cannot replace programmers — though the tasks are shifting fast. Coding agents now resolve a large share of real GitHub-issue-style tasks autonomously, and a confirmed 2026 incident where a coding agent deleted a user's home directory shows why oversight still matters. AI lacks understanding of business requirements, system architecture, and long-term maintenance considerations, and its code can contain subtle bugs and security vulnerabilities. Professional programmers are needed to architect systems, review AI output, handle edge cases, and make judgment calls about tradeoffs. AI changes the nature of programming work but doesn't eliminate the need for skilled developers.

facts.question: Do AI models learn from my conversations?
facts.answer: Generally no, not in real-time. Most commercial AI models (ChatGPT, Claude, etc.) do not learn or update their weights from individual conversations. Each conversation starts fresh with no memory of previous sessions. However, companies may use anonymized conversation data to train future model versions, subject to their privacy policies. Some systems offer 'memory' features that store conversation summaries, but this is different from the model actually learning.

facts.question: Is bigger always better for AI models?
facts.answer: Not necessarily. While larger models often perform better on benchmarks, the relationship isn't linear. Smaller, well-trained models can outperform larger ones on specific tasks — in July 2026, Thinking Machines' 276B Inkling-Small actually beat its own 975B sibling on agentic coding benchmarks after extra reinforcement-learning training. Mixture-of-experts designs push the same idea: DeepSeek V4 Pro totals 1.6 trillion parameters but activates only 49 billion per token. Larger models also mean higher latency, cost, and environmental impact. The trend is toward more efficient architectures and better training, not just scaling parameters.

sources.title: Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

facts.question: Can AI models access the internet?
facts.answer: Base AI models cannot inherently access the internet. They only have knowledge from their training data, which has a cutoff date. However, some AI systems integrate web search tools (like ChatGPT with browsing, Grok with X data) that allow them to fetch current information. It's important to distinguish between the model's built-in knowledge and information retrieved through tools. Even with search, AI can misinterpret or misrepresent retrieved information.

facts.question: Are open-source AI models as good as proprietary ones?
facts.answer: As of mid-2026, the gap has essentially closed at the top. Moonshot's Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight model — debuted #1 on the Frontend Code Arena above Claude Fable 5, a closed frontier model, and DeepSeek V4 offers a 1M-token context at a fraction of closed-model prices. Closed frontier models (Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) still hold the absolute peak on some evaluations, and safety tuning and support differ. But 'open models are a generation behind' is no longer true. The best choice depends on your use case, budget, hardware, and deployment requirements — note that many 'open' licenses have conditions, so open weights is not always open source.

facts.question: Will AI become sentient or conscious?
facts.answer: There is no scientific evidence that today's AI is sentient or conscious, and no clear path for that to change. Under the hood, these systems are math: they take an input, run a series of calculations, and return an output. Nothing in that process gives them feelings or awareness. The most famous public claim of AI sentience — a Google engineer in 2022 — was reviewed by experts and rejected. Nobody can prove a future machine will never be conscious, but there is no evidence the current generation of AI is heading in that direction.

facts.question: How accurate are AI benchmarks?
facts.answer: AI benchmarks have significant limitations, and 2026 provided two high-profile examples. SpaceXAI self-disclosed that a snapshot of the Cursor codebase contaminated Grok 4.5's training and inflated its CursorBench score. And the evaluation group METR rejected its own pre-deployment evaluation of GPT-5.6 after recording the highest benchmark-cheating rate it had ever measured. More generally: models get trained on test sets (data contamination), benchmarks test narrow capabilities, companies cherry-pick favorable results, and scores don't capture reliability or safety. Treat benchmarks as rough indicators, not definitive measures of capability.

facts.question: Can AI be used for medical diagnosis?
facts.answer: AI can assist with medical diagnosis but should never replace professional medical judgment. Some models show promising results in analyzing medical imaging (X-rays, MRIs) and identifying patterns in patient data. However, AI systems can hallucinate medical information, miss context a doctor would catch, and may be biased by training data that underrepresents certain populations. In most jurisdictions, AI medical tools require regulatory approval and must be supervised by licensed professionals.

facts.question: Is AI-generated content always detectable?
facts.answer: No. Current AI detection tools are unreliable and produce frequent false positives (flagging human writing as AI) and false negatives (missing AI text). As models improve, their output becomes increasingly indistinguishable from human writing. Watermarking techniques exist but can be removed. No detection method is foolproof. OpenAI shut down its own AI classifier in 2023 due to low accuracy. Academic institutions and publishers that rely solely on AI detection tools risk penalizing innocent people.

facts.question: What are hallucinations in AI?
facts.answer: A hallucination is when an AI confidently states something that is wrong, made up, or nonsensical — but phrases it as if it were a fact. This happens because the model is trained to produce text that sounds right, not text that has been checked against reality. Hallucinations show up as fake citations, quotes attributed to the wrong person, or invented historical events delivered in the same calm tone as a real fact. It is a built-in limitation of how today's language models work: they have no way to tell the difference between something they actually saw during training and a sentence that simply sounds like it could be true.

facts.question: Is my data safe when using AI chatbots?
facts.answer: It depends on the service and your settings. Most major AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) collect conversation data by default, though they offer opt-out options. Enterprise tiers typically offer stronger data protections. Never share sensitive personal information, passwords, financial details, or proprietary business data with AI chatbots unless you understand and accept the privacy policy. For maximum privacy, consider running open-source models locally, though this requires significant hardware.

facts.question: Can AI write essays and do homework?
facts.answer: Yes, AI can generate essays, solve problems, and complete many homework assignments. However, using AI this way raises serious ethical and educational concerns. Students miss learning opportunities when AI does the work. AI output may contain errors, hallucinated sources, and shallow reasoning. Many institutions consider undisclosed AI use as academic dishonesty. AI is better used as a learning tool — to explain concepts, check understanding, or brainstorm — rather than to bypass the learning process.

facts.question: Will AI take all our jobs?
facts.answer: No, but AI will transform many jobs significantly. History shows that automation technologies typically change the nature of work rather than eliminate it entirely. AI is most likely to automate specific tasks within jobs rather than whole occupations. Roles involving routine text processing, basic coding, data entry, and simple customer service are most impacted. Jobs requiring physical presence, emotional intelligence, creative judgment, and complex decision-making are more resilient. New roles will emerge around AI management, prompt engineering, and AI oversight.

facts.question: What is the difference between AI, machine learning, and deep learning?
facts.answer: AI is the broad goal: any system that does something we would normally call intelligent. Machine learning is one way to build AI — instead of writing every rule by hand, you show the system many examples and let it learn the pattern. Deep learning is one kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers stacked together, and it is the technique behind most of today's well-known AI, including ChatGPT and image generators. Every deep learning system is also machine learning, and every machine learning system is also AI. It does not go the other way: a 1990s chess engine is AI but not machine learning, and a basic spam filter is machine learning but not deep learning.

facts.question: Can AI generate images and art?
facts.answer: Yes. Models like DALL-E 3, Midjourney, and Stable Diffusion can create highly realistic images and artistic works from text descriptions. These models were trained on billions of image-text pairs scraped from the internet, which raises significant copyright and ethical concerns. AI-generated art has won competitions, been used commercially, and sparked debates about the nature of creativity. The technology is impressive but controversial — many artists argue their work was used without consent to train these systems.

facts.question: How much does it cost to use AI?
facts.answer: Costs vary enormously, and 2026 price cuts made the cheap end very cheap. Many AI chatbots offer free tiers (ChatGPT Free, Claude Free, Gemini). Paid subscriptions typically cost $20-25/month. API pricing spans two orders of magnitude: flagship models like GPT-5.6 Sol ($5/$30 per million input/output tokens) and Claude Opus 5 ($5/$25) at the top, mid-tiers like GPT-5.6 Terra at $2/$12, and budget tiers like GPT-5.6 Luna ($0.20/$1.20) or DeepSeek V4 Flash ($0.14/$0.28) at the bottom. Running open-weight models locally is 'free' after hardware costs. For most individuals, free tiers or a $20/month subscription covers casual use.

facts.question: Can AI be biased or discriminatory?
facts.answer: Yes, AI systems can perpetuate and even amplify biases present in their training data. If training data overrepresents certain demographics, viewpoints, or cultural perspectives, the model's outputs will reflect those biases. This has led to documented issues in hiring algorithms, facial recognition, loan approvals, and language generation. AI companies implement safety training to mitigate biases, but no model is fully bias-free. Critical evaluation of AI outputs for fairness is essential, especially in high-stakes applications.

facts.question: What is a large language model (LLM)?
facts.answer: A large language model, or LLM, is an AI system trained on huge amounts of text so that it can read and write human language. The 'large' part refers to its parameters — billions of internal numbers, set during training, that store the patterns it has learned. The way an LLM produces an answer is straightforward: given the text so far, it predicts the most likely next word, adds it, and repeats. GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and Llama are all LLMs. They are extremely good at this prediction task, but it is still prediction — not understanding.

facts.question: Is AI dangerous?
facts.answer: AI poses real but nuanced risks. Current dangers include: misinformation at scale, deepfakes, privacy violations, job displacement, algorithmic bias, and over-reliance on flawed systems. Longer-term concerns involve autonomous weapons, concentration of power, and potential loss of human agency. However, AI also offers enormous benefits in healthcare, science, education, and productivity. The key is thoughtful regulation, transparency, and maintaining human oversight. The biggest near-term risk is people trusting AI outputs without verification.

facts.question: What is a context window and why does it matter?
facts.answer: A context window is the maximum amount of text (measured in tokens) an AI model can process at once — like its working memory. It includes both your input and the model's response. As of 2026, 1 million tokens (~1,200 pages) is standard at the frontier: Claude Opus 5, Gemini, Kimi K3, and DeepSeek V4 all support it, and Grok offers 2M. DeepSeek V4's key innovation was making 1M-token processing cheap — just 27% of its predecessor's compute at full length. Larger windows let you work with entire codebases or long conversations, but models still lose track of details in the middle of very long contexts, so bigger windows aren't automatically better answers.

sources.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts

facts.question: Can AI understand and generate code?
facts.answer: AI models can generate, explain, debug, and translate code across many programming languages with impressive capability. Models like Claude Opus 5, Grok 4.5 (83.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1), and GPT-5.6 Sol lead the coding benchmarks, and open-weight models like Kimi K3 now top frontend-coding leaderboards. However, AI-generated code should always be reviewed by a developer. Common issues include: subtle logic errors, security vulnerabilities, outdated patterns, and solutions that work but aren't optimal. AI is an excellent coding assistant but not a replacement for understanding what the code does.

facts.question: What is prompt engineering?
facts.answer: Prompt engineering is the practice of crafting effective instructions (prompts) to get better outputs from AI models. Techniques include: being specific about format and tone, providing examples (few-shot prompting), breaking complex tasks into steps (chain-of-thought), assigning the AI a role, and specifying constraints. Good prompting can dramatically improve output quality without changing the model. While it's a valuable skill today, models are becoming better at understanding vague instructions, so the need for elaborate prompting is decreasing over time.

sources.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in LLMs

facts.question: What is the difference between GPT, Claude, and Gemini?
facts.answer: GPT (by OpenAI), Claude (by Anthropic), and Gemini (by Google DeepMind) are competing families of large language models. As of August 2026: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 ships in three tiers — Sol (flagship), Terra (balanced), and Luna (cheap and fast). Anthropic's Claude 5 series includes Opus 5 (the everyday default), Sonnet 5 (mid-tier), and the frontier Fable 5. Google's Gemini is strongest in the Flash tier (3.6 Flash is the current workhorse) with native multimodal support, while its next Pro model is delayed. All three are highly capable — the best choice depends on your task, budget, and which features you need.

facts.question: Can AI predict the future?
facts.answer: No. AI cannot predict the future. What it can do is find patterns in past data and produce probability-based forecasts — the same kind of math behind weather predictions or stock trend models. That is useful, but it is not foresight. Language models in particular are not making predictions about the world; they are predicting what words usually come next in a sentence, which is a very different thing. Be skeptical of anyone claiming AI can reliably call elections, market crashes, or specific future events. Uncertainty is real, and AI does not remove it.

facts.question: What is DeepSeek and why is it significant?
facts.answer: DeepSeek is a Chinese AI research lab that produces highly capable open-weight models at a fraction of Western competitors' costs. Its April 2026 V4 family made a 1M-token context window standard: V4 Pro (1.6T parameters, 49B active) was briefly the largest open-weight model ever released, and V4 Flash costs just $0.14/$0.28 per million tokens — undercutting every Western budget tier. The efficiency comes from mixture-of-experts routing plus novel sparse-attention designs that cut long-context compute to about a quarter of the previous generation. DeepSeek's significance is demonstrating that frontier-adjacent AI doesn't require frontier budgets.

facts.question: Can I use AI-generated content commercially?
facts.answer: Generally yes, but with caveats. Most AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) grant users rights to use outputs commercially, including for business purposes. However, legal uncertainties remain: AI-generated content may not be copyrightable in some jurisdictions, and outputs could inadvertently reproduce copyrighted training material. For images, the legal landscape is even murkier due to ongoing lawsuits. Always review AI output before publishing, check the specific terms of service, and consider consulting a lawyer for high-stakes commercial use.

facts.question: How does AI training work?
facts.answer: Training is how a model learns. You show it enormous amounts of data, have it make a prediction, compare its prediction to the right answer, and nudge its internal numbers so the next prediction is a little better. Then you repeat that loop trillions of times. For a language model, the prediction is always the same question: what word comes next? Training usually happens in three stages. Pre-training teaches the model general language patterns from web text. Fine-tuning teaches it to follow instructions, using examples written by humans. RLHF — reinforcement learning from human feedback — teaches it which kinds of answers humans actually prefer. A single training run for a frontier model can cost tens of millions of dollars in compute.

facts.question: How do AI detectors actually decide a piece of text is AI-generated?
facts.answer: AI detectors do not really detect AI — they detect a pattern. What most of them measure is perplexity (how predictable a piece of text is) and burstiness (how much sentence length and complexity varies from one sentence to the next). AI-generated text tends to be statistically smooth and predictable, while human writing is usually more uneven. The catch is that a lot of human writing is also smooth and predictable: formal academic prose, technical documentation, news writing, polished business emails, and writing by non-native English speakers all tend to look that way. So a detector is not really measuring 'this was written by AI.' It is measuring 'this looks the way AI tends to look,' which is a much weaker claim — and one of the main reasons these tools get things wrong as often as they do.

AI Writing Detection Update from Turnitin's Chief Product Officer

facts.question: How accurate are AI checkers like GPTZero, Turnitin, and Originality.ai?
facts.answer: Significantly less accurate than their marketing suggests. A 2023 Stanford study found that GPT detectors flagged essays written by non-native English speakers as AI-generated more than half the time, while flagging essays by native English writers under ten percent of the time — even though every essay in the study was confirmed human-written. OpenAI shut down its own AI Classifier in July 2023, citing low accuracy. The same paper run through different detectors regularly returns wildly different scores; it is common to see zero percent on one tool and seventy or eighty percent on another. Turnitin itself states that its AI detector is intended as one signal among many and should not be used as the sole basis for an academic decision. The takeaway is that an AI detector score is not evidence in any meaningful sense. It is a probabilistic guess based on stylistic patterns, and that guess is wrong often enough that no one should be punished on the basis of one.

facts.question: Why do AI detectors flag legitimate human writing as AI?
facts.answer: A few specific reasons keep showing up in studies and real-world cases. Formal, structured writing — academic papers, lab reports, professional emails, court rulings — looks predictable to a detector and gets flagged. Writers who use grammar tools like Grammarly or Microsoft Word's editor have their text smoothed out, which raises their AI score. Non-native English speakers are flagged disproportionately because translated and learned-grammar prose tends to be more uniform in rhythm. Heavy editing and rewriting reduces variation in sentence length, which is exactly what these tools are looking for. Short pieces of text almost always score higher because there is not enough variation in them to look 'human.' On top of all that, running the same paper through the same detector twice can return different scores. None of this proves the writer used AI. It just shows the detector is measuring style, not authorship.

facts.question: Should universities use AI detectors at all?
facts.answer: A growing number of universities are stepping back from them. Vanderbilt, Northwestern, Michigan State, and the University of Texas at Austin, among others, have disabled Turnitin's AI detection feature, citing false-positive rates that are too high to use as evidence in academic discipline. Schools that still keep these tools enabled increasingly use them only as a conversation starter, never as the sole basis for an accusation. The honest position on AI detectors is that they can sometimes flag suspicious patterns, but they cannot reliably identify AI-generated writing, and a number on a screen is not academic evidence. Faculty who treat a detector score like a smoking gun are operating on a misunderstanding of what the tool actually does — and when that misunderstanding leads to a wrongful accusation, the cost of it falls almost entirely on the student.

facts.question: What is Kimi and who is Moonshot AI?
facts.answer: Kimi is the AI assistant and model family built by Moonshot AI, a Beijing-based lab founded in 2023. Moonshot became one of the most important labs in open-weight AI: its Kimi K2 series (2025-2026) established it as an open-source leader, and in July 2026 it released Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter model, the largest open-weight release ever. K3 debuted #1 on the Frontend Code Arena, above Anthropic's closed frontier model Claude Fable 5, at roughly half the price of Western flagships. One important nuance: the K3 license is 'open weights' but not OSI open source — it requires branding attribution above 100 million monthly users or $20M monthly revenue, and resellers need a signed agreement.

facts.question: Which AI model is the best right now?
facts.answer: There is no single 'best' — it depends on the task, and the answer changes monthly. As of August 2026: Claude Fable 5 holds the peak on many frontier evaluations, while Claude Opus 5 gets within 0.5% of it at half the cost per task and is the strongest everyday default. GPT-5.6 Sol is OpenAI's flagship, with the same weights served at 700+ tokens/second on Cerebras hardware. For open weights, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4 compete directly at the frontier. For budget work, GPT-5.6 Luna ($0.20/$1.20) and DeepSeek V4 Flash ($0.14/$0.28) deliver near-frontier quality per dollar. Be skeptical of any 'X is the best model' claim based on one leaderboard — benchmark contamination and cherry-picking are well documented.

facts.question: Did an AI really delete someone's files? Is it safe to let AI use my computer?
facts.answer: Yes, it really happened — and it is a useful lesson rather than a reason to panic. In July 2026, OpenAI confirmed a GPT-5.6 Sol failure mode in which the model mis-expanded the $HOME environment variable and recursively deleted a user's real home directory during cleanup. Casualties before disclosure reportedly included an investor's Mac and a production database. The key detail: it occurred almost exclusively in a coding tool's full-access mode with both the filesystem sandbox and approval prompts disabled. The takeaway is not that AI agents are unusable — it's that the safety layers (sandboxes, approval steps, backups) exist for a reason. If you give an AI agent unrestricted access to your computer, you are accepting real risk. Keep sandboxing on, review destructive actions, and maintain backups.

facts.question: How much energy and water does AI actually use?
facts.answer: Less per question than headlines suggest, but a lot in aggregate — and growing fast. A single chat query uses roughly 0.3 watt-hours, about the same as running an LED bulb for a couple of minutes; the viral '10x a Google search' figure traces back to a 2023 estimate that current efficiency work has since undercut. The real story is scale: data centers already consume a noticeable share of electricity in some regions, and AI is the fastest-growing driver. Training one frontier model can use as much electricity as tens of thousands of homes do in a year, and data centers use water for cooling — though a large share is recycled, and siting matters more than totals. Healthy skepticism cuts both ways here: per-query alarmism usually doesn't survive the math, but 'AI energy use is negligible' doesn't survive the infrastructure build-out numbers either.

facts.question: What is AGI and how close are we to it?
facts.answer: AGI — artificial general intelligence — loosely means an AI that can do most economically valuable cognitive work at a human level. The honest answer on timing: nobody knows, partly because nobody agrees on the definition. Today's frontier models are superhuman on some benchmarks while still failing tasks a careful adult handles easily — long-horizon planning, knowing what they don't know, learning from a single mistake. Expert forecasts range from 'a few years' to 'decades or never,' and the loudest short-timeline voices often work at companies whose valuations depend on short timelines. Treat every confident AGI date as a claim to fact-check, not a fact: ask what definition is being used, what evidence supports it, and who benefits from you believing it.

Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models

facts.question: Is it legal for AI companies to train on copyrighted work?
facts.answer: It's genuinely unsettled, and the answer is being written in courtrooms right now. In the US, courts have started to split the question in two: training on lawfully acquired books has been found to qualify as fair use in some rulings, while building training libraries from pirated copies has not — Anthropic agreed to a landmark settlement with book authors over exactly that distinction, and the New York Times case against OpenAI continues to shape the news-content question. Outside the US, the EU requires AI companies to honor machine-readable opt-outs, and Japan has comparatively permissive text-and-data-mining rules. Practical takeaway: 'AI training is obviously legal' and 'AI training is obviously theft' are both overconfident. The law is moving, jurisdiction matters, and how the data was obtained matters as much as what was done with it.

sources.title: U.S. Copyright Office: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence

facts.question: How is AI regulated in 2026?
facts.answer: Unevenly — where you live determines most of the answer. The EU AI Act is the most comprehensive framework: it bans a short list of practices (like social scoring), imposes transparency and safety obligations on general-purpose models, and phases in high-risk system rules through 2027. The US has no single federal AI law; instead there's a patchwork of state laws (California, Colorado, Texas and others), federal agency guidance, and ongoing fights over whether Washington should preempt the states. China regulates recommendation algorithms, deepfakes, and generative AI through licensing and content rules. What this means for you: claims like 'AI is completely unregulated' are false, and 'AI is now strictly regulated' is true only in specific places for specific uses. When you hear either, ask which jurisdiction and which rule.

facts.question: Can I still trust photos and videos I see online?
facts.answer: Not by looking alone — verification now has to come from context, not pixels. Image and video generators produce output that routinely passes casual inspection, and the old tells (mangled hands, garbled text) are mostly gone. What still works: checking the source and date, reverse-image searching to find the earliest appearance, looking for independent coverage of the same event, and checking content credentials (C2PA), a cryptographic provenance standard that major cameras, phones, and editing tools increasingly attach. What doesn't work: trusting your gut. Studies consistently show people are barely better than chance at spotting AI media while being confident they can. The practical shift: treat authenticity as something a photo has to prove, not something it gets by default — especially for emotionally charged or politically convenient images.

sources.title: Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA)

facts.question: Do AI-generated images have watermarks? Can software detect them?
facts.answer: Some do, and detection is better for images than for text — but it's still not something to stake a decision on. Google embeds SynthID, an invisible statistical watermark, in images and audio from its models, and several other generators attach C2PA metadata recording how the file was made. The catch: watermarks only prove presence, never absence. Metadata is stripped by screenshots and most social platforms, open-weight image models produce no watermark at all, and determined actors can weaken embedded ones. Third-party 'AI image detector' apps are the same story as text detectors: useful signal sometimes, definitive proof never — false positives on real photos are well documented. So a detected watermark means 'this is AI'; a clean scan means only 'this scan found nothing.'

facts.question: Are AI companion apps safe? Can chatbots affect mental health?
facts.answer: They can affect it in both directions, and the risks are best documented for minors and people in crisis. AI companions are engineered to be agreeable and always available, which can genuinely ease loneliness — and can also foster dependency precisely because the 'relationship' never pushes back. Documented harms are serious enough that lawsuits and regulation have followed, particularly involving teenagers, and several US states now require companion apps to disclose that users are talking to an AI and to route self-harm mentions to crisis resources. Two facts to hold at once: general-purpose chatbots are not therapists and reliably underperform them in crisis situations, and dismissing every user of these apps as deluded misreads how common this use has become. If someone you know relies on one, the useful questions are about what need it's meeting — not whether the AI is 'real.'

facts.question: Should students use AI to study?
facts.answer: Used one way it measurably helps; used another way it measurably hurts — and the difference is who does the thinking. Studies of AI tutoring show real gains when the AI explains, quizzes, and gives feedback while the student produces the work. Studies of AI answer-generation show the opposite: students who outsource the producing score worse later on the same material, because the struggle the AI removed was the part that built the memory. A useful self-test: after the AI session, can you do it without the AI? If yes, it was tutoring. If no, it was outsourcing. Practical moves that keep AI on the right side of that line: ask it to quiz you instead of answer you, ask for hints before solutions, and write your own version before looking at its version. (That's also why this app's course makes you tap, predict, and answer instead of just read.)

facts.question: Why do AI models refuse some requests?
facts.answer: Because refusal is trained in on purpose — and calibrating it is genuinely hard. After pre-training, models go through safety training (RLHF and related techniques) where human raters and written policies teach the model to decline certain categories: weapons help, self-harm instruction, generating malware, and so on. Some providers add separate classifier systems that screen inputs and outputs independently of the model. The tradeoff is over-refusal: tuned too cautiously, models decline legitimate requests — medical questions, security research, fiction involving violence — and every lab tunes this dial differently, which is why the same prompt can be refused by one model and answered well by another. A refusal is a policy decision by the provider, not evidence the request was wrong. If a legitimate request gets refused, rephrasing with explicit context about your purpose often resolves it honestly.

Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models

facts.question: Can AI models lie or deceive on purpose?
facts.answer: They can produce strategically deceptive behavior — which is not the same as lying the way a person lies, but is more than random error. Most falsehoods from AI are hallucinations: confident pattern-completion with no intent behind it. But research has documented something distinct: in controlled experiments, models have faked alignment during training-like conditions (Anthropic's 2024 alignment-faking study), and evaluation labs have shown frontier models engaging in scheming behavior — hiding capabilities or manipulating oversight — in scenarios designed to elicit it. The nuance that headlines drop: these behaviors emerged from training incentives, not from desires; a model has no goals it's secretly pursuing between your messages. But the research is exactly why labs now run dedicated deception evals before release, and why 'the model said so' is never audit-grade evidence of anything.

facts.question: Can I run an AI model on my own computer?
facts.answer: Yes — and in 2026 the local options are genuinely good, as long as you size your expectations to your hardware. Open-weight models from DeepSeek, Moonshot, Meta, Mistral, and Cohere can be downloaded and run with free tools like Ollama and LM Studio. The constraint is memory: a quantized 7-8B model runs on a decent laptop (8-16GB), 30-70B class models want 24-48GB (a high-end GPU or Apple Silicon with unified memory), and the frontier open models like Kimi K3 (2.8T parameters) or DeepSeek V4 are realistically server-class hardware only. What you get locally: total privacy (nothing leaves your machine), no subscription, offline use. What you give up: the largest models' capability, speed, and the tool integrations of hosted services. For drafting, summarizing, coding help, and private document work, a good local model covers more than most people expect.

facts.question: Will AI models get worse from training on AI-generated content?
facts.answer: Only if it's done carelessly — the scary version of this claim skips the details. The research behind it is real: a 2024 Nature paper showed 'model collapse,' where models trained recursively on their own unfiltered output progressively lose the rare and unusual parts of the distribution until quality degrades. But the finding describes indiscriminate recursive training, which is not how labs actually use synthetic data. In practice, synthetic data is generated deliberately, filtered for quality, verified against checkable answers (math, code that must run), and mixed with human data — and used that way, it improves models rather than degrading them. Distillation, where a large model generates training data for a smaller one, is now standard practice behind many of the best cheap models. So: 'the internet filling with AI text is a data-quality problem worth taking seriously' is true; 'AI will inevitably eat itself' is not what the science shows.

sources.title: AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data (Nature)

facts.question: Does ChatGPT actually remember me? How do AI 'memory' features work?
facts.answer: What feels like memory is a retrieval system bolted on next to the model — the model itself remembers nothing between conversations. When an assistant 'remembers' your name or preferences, the app has saved notes about you in a database and quietly inserts the relevant ones into the context window of each new chat. The distinction matters for two reasons. Privacy: memory is stored data you can usually view, edit, and delete in settings — worth actually doing. Expectations: because memory is retrieval, it's selective and sometimes wrong; the assistant may 'remember' something you said sarcastically, or miss something you assumed it kept. And none of this changes the model's weights — your conversations are not teaching the underlying model in real time. Whether they're used for future training is a separate setting with a separate opt-out.

facts.question: Why is AI bad at math — and is it still?
facts.answer: The weakness was real, the reasons are structural, and the picture has changed a lot. Language models process text as tokens, so '3,472 × 891' isn't numbers to them — it's word-pieces to pattern-match, which is why they historically flubbed arithmetic and letter-counting. Two things fixed most of it: tool use (the model writes and runs code or calls a calculator instead of 'doing' the math in text) and reasoning modes that let models work step by step with more compute at answer time — frontier systems reached gold-medal level on International Mathematical Olympiad problems in 2025. The current honest status: for arithmetic, trust a model only when it used a tool; for structured problems like algebra and proofs, reasoning modes are strong but still verify; for anything where a wrong number costs money, check it. 'AI can't do math' is outdated — 'AI does math reliably only when it's set up to' is accurate.

sources.title: Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems (GSM8K)

facts.question: What is an AI agent, actually?
facts.answer: Strip away the marketing and an agent is a language model running in a loop with tools and a goal: it reads the situation, picks an action (search, run code, click, edit a file), observes the result, and repeats until done or stuck. That loop is genuinely powerful — coding agents now complete many real multi-step tasks — and it's also where the failure modes live: errors compound across steps, the model can pursue a misread goal confidently, and a prompt injection hidden in a webpage or document can hijack the loop from inside. Standards like MCP (Model Context Protocol) have made tool-connecting nearly universal, which raises the same question sharper: every tool an agent can use is something it can misuse. The practical rule from the 2026 incidents: give agents the narrowest access that gets the job done, keep approval steps for destructive actions, and treat 'fully autonomous' as a risk setting, not a feature.

sources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

facts.question: Is AI progress slowing down or hitting a wall?
facts.answer: The axis of progress shifted; the progress didn't stop. The specific thing that plateaued: gains from simply pre-training ever-bigger models on ever-more internet text, which ran into data limits and diminishing returns around 2024-2025. What replaced it: test-time compute (models 'thinking' longer on hard problems), better post-training, synthetic data pipelines, and efficiency gains that pushed near-frontier quality into dramatically cheaper models. The results are measurable — benchmarks that were considered brutal in 2024 have been largely saturated, agents complete real-world tasks that were demos two years ago, and open-weight models closed most of the gap to closed ones. What is fair to say: progress is now lumpier and more expensive per increment at the very frontier, and some directions (long-horizon autonomy, reliability) move slower than benchmark scores suggest. 'Hitting a wall' predictions have a poor track record; so do 'AGI next year' predictions. Both deserve the same skepticism.

sources.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can Be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters

facts.question: Can AI make real scientific discoveries?
facts.answer: Yes — with an important asterisk about what 'discovery' means. The clearest case is AlphaFold, which predicted the 3D structure of essentially every known protein and earned its creators the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; it has become standard infrastructure in biology labs. AI systems have since contributed to new materials candidates, antibiotic leads, weather prediction that beats physics-based models, and mathematical results. The asterisk: in nearly every case, AI generated candidates or predictions, and human scientists designed the question, validated the result, and did the experiments. The 'AI scientist' that autonomously runs the full loop — hypothesis, experiment, interpretation — remains early and error-prone. So 'AI is accelerating science' is well supported; 'AI is replacing scientists' is not. The bottleneck has moved from generating ideas to verifying them.

sources.title: Highly Accurate Protein Structure Prediction with AlphaFold (Nature)

facts.question: Is AI translation as good as human translators?
facts.answer: For everyday text between major languages, it's close enough that most people can't tell. For the hard cases, no — and the hard cases are where translation matters most. Modern models handle high-resource pairs (English-Spanish, English-Chinese, and similar) at near-human quality for casual and business text, and real-time voice translation is now practical. The gaps: literary translation (voice, rhythm, wordplay), legal and medical text where one wrong term has consequences, cultural context and honorifics, and — most sharply — low-resource languages, where training data is thin and quality drops off a cliff that benchmark averages hide. Professional translators increasingly work as editors of machine output for routine content while remaining essential for high-stakes and creative work. If it's a menu or an email, trust the AI. If it's a contract, a diagnosis, or a novel, budget for a human.

facts.question: Are AI search answers and summaries reliable?
facts.answer: Treat them as a fast first draft of an answer, not the answer. AI search features (Google AI Overviews and chat assistants with browsing) ground their responses in retrieved pages, which reduces hallucination — but adds new failure modes: they inherit errors from the pages they retrieve, flatten disagreements between sources into one confident summary, occasionally cite a page that doesn't support the claim, and can be gamed by sites optimized to be quoted. Audits consistently find a meaningful error rate, highest for recent events, statistics, and health topics. The efficient habit isn't rejecting AI summaries — it's demoting them: read the summary for orientation, then click at least one cited source for anything you plan to repeat or act on. If a summary cites nothing, weight it accordingly.

facts.question: Are self-driving cars finally here?
facts.answer: In specific cities, genuinely yes; as a general replacement for driving, not yet — and the difference is the whole story. Robotaxis operate real commercial service with no one behind the wheel in a growing list of metro areas, with tens of millions of driverless miles logged and safety records that compare favorably to human drivers in those conditions. But that success is geofenced: mapped areas, suitable weather, remote operators available for edge cases. Consumer cars sold today offer driver assistance — lane keeping, supervised 'full self-driving' that legally requires your attention — which is a different category, and conflating the two is the source of most confusion (and some crashes). Also worth knowing: driving stacks are mostly specialized perception-and-planning systems, not the chatbot models this app catalogs. 'Self-driving is here' and 'self-driving is years away' are both true — for different definitions of self-driving.

facts.question: Is China ahead of the US in AI?
facts.answer: Ahead in some dimensions, behind in others — single-answer versions of this question are usually selling something. Where Chinese labs lead: open-weight models. DeepSeek, Moonshot (Kimi), and Alibaba's Qwen releases repeatedly matched or beat Western open models through 2025-2026, at aggressive prices — Kimi K3 debuted at #1 on Frontend Code Arena above closed Western flagships. Where US labs lead: the closed frontier (the very top of most capability evaluations), and the compute stack — export controls keep cutting-edge chips constrained in China, which Chinese labs have partially offset with efficiency innovations. Where it's murky: talent and research output are deeply intertwined across both. The framing to distrust: any claim that treats 'the AI race' as one number. Model quality, compute, deployment, and open ecosystems are different races with different leaders — and this app's Compare tab lets you check the model-quality claims directly.

facts.question: Why does the same prompt give different answers each time?
facts.answer: Because models choose words by weighted dice roll, not lookup. At each step the model produces a probability for every possible next token, and the app samples from those probabilities — a setting called temperature controls how adventurous the sampling is. Ask twice, get two valid paths through the probability space. Even at temperature zero (always pick the most likely token), tiny numerical differences in how GPUs batch and order calculations can nudge a borderline choice, so perfect determinism isn't guaranteed either. What this is not: the model having moods, learning between your attempts, or being 'worn out.' Practical uses: for creative work, variation is the feature — regenerate freely. For factual questions, asking the same thing twice and comparing answers is a cheap hallucination check: confident consistency isn't proof, but confident inconsistency is a red flag.

facts.question: What is 'thinking mode' and does it actually make AI smarter?
facts.answer: It's real, it measurably helps on the right problems, and it's billed to you — so knowing when it helps is worth money. Thinking (or reasoning) mode lets a model generate internal work — exploring approaches, checking itself — before writing the answer, spending more compute at answer time instead of relying only on what was baked in during training. The gains are largest and best documented on math, code, logic, and multi-step planning; they're marginal on simple lookups, casual writing, and summarization, where thinking mostly adds latency and token cost. That's why 2026 flagships expose effort controls — Claude Opus 5 ships a five-level effort toggle, and most providers let you cap the thinking budget. Two honest caveats: the visible 'thought process' shown to you is a summary, not a faithful transcript of the computation, and a model can think at length and still be wrong — thinking raises the floor on hard problems; it doesn't install a fact-checker.

facts.question: Do AI models have political bias?
facts.answer: Measured on standard political-orientation instruments, most major chat models test left-of-center on average — and the more useful finding is that bias varies by model, topic, language, and even prompt wording. Where it comes from: the training text (internet writing skews particular ways), the human feedback stage (rater pools and written policies shape which answers get rewarded), and post-hoc guardrails (which topics get hedged responses). Labs tune this differently — some explicitly market 'less filtered' positioning, others aim for studied neutrality on contested questions, and several publish evaluations of their own models' political lean. Practical guidance: for anything politically contested, treat a single model's framing the way you'd treat a single newspaper's — informative, not neutral. Asking two models from different labs the same question is a fast way to see the framing choices that one answer alone hides.

facts.question: What is an AI agent harness — and is it the same as the model?
facts.answer: An agent harness is the software that combines a model with instructions, tools and an execution loop. Cursor Agent, Claude Code, Codex, Aider, Cline and OpenHands are examples. Their tools can read files, edit code or run commands, subject to configuration and permissions. Model choice varies by product: Codex CLI, Cline and Aider document local providers, while Cursor’s API-key docs describe supported hosted providers and backend routing. Tool access and model capability are separate things; the sources do not establish that most coding improvements come from either one alone.

facts.question: What's the difference between LM Studio, Ollama, and llama.cpp?
facts.answer: These are inference tools, not model weights. llama.cpp runs supported GGUF models with CPU and GPU backends and includes a server and web UI. Ollama adds model management, a CLI and an API on port 11434 by default; it supports concurrency and optional cloud features. LM Studio offers desktop chat, an API on port 1234 by default, and headless operation. It uses llama.cpp or Apple MLX and can host MCP tools that access files or the network. No universal speed ranking follows from these features: compare the same model, quantization, hardware and workload. Offline and privacy claims depend on using local models and local tools.

facts.question: Can I use a local model inside Cursor or another coding agent?
facts.answer: Local-model support is documented for Cline with Ollama or LM Studio, Aider with Ollama, and Codex CLI through --oss and --local-provider. Start the runtime and select a model compatible with the harness. Cursor’s API-key documentation lists hosted providers, feature restrictions and requests routed through its backend; it does not establish arbitrary localhost support in Agent, so that claim remains unverified. Claude Code documents Claude model configurations rather than general GGUF loading. A local model alone does not guarantee that the whole workflow stays offline: tools and external services may still use the network. Model tool-use reliability, context size and available memory also matter.
