sections.content: That's what AI Fact Checker is for! Take the Knowledge Check quiz on the Learn page to lock in the vocabulary. Browse Companies for verified model specs and myth-vs-fact breakdowns. Use Fact Check to search for answers, Compare to weigh models side by side, and press ⌘K anytime to search everything. And always check our Sources.

lessons.keyTakeaway: Healthy skepticism is your best tool. If a claim sounds too good (or too scary) to be true, it probably is. This app is here to help you verify.

advancedLessons.title: Inside the Transformer
advancedLessons.subtitle: What actually happens between your prompt and the answer.

sections.content: In the fundamentals course you learned that models read tokens and predict the next one. This lesson opens the box: nearly every model in this app — GPT, Claude, Gemini, Kimi, DeepSeek — is a transformer, an architecture introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need.' Understanding its three moving parts explains many model behaviors that otherwise seem mysterious.

sources.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017)

sections.heading: The Assembly Line
sections.content: A transformer processes your text in a repeating cycle. Each token becomes a vector (a long list of numbers), and then dozens of identical layers refine those vectors, each layer mixing in more context. Run a forward pass through the stack:

visual.caption: One forward pass — this whole climb happens once per generated token

sections.heading: Attention, Without the Math
sections.content: Attention is the transformer's signature move. For every token, the model asks: which other tokens in the context matter for understanding this one? Attention computes a relevance score between every pair of tokens and blends information accordingly — in parallel, across many independent 'heads' that each learn different relationship types: grammar, coreference, topic, position. Explore a real example:

visual.caption: Simplified single-head view — real models run dozens of heads like this in parallel, per layer

sections.heading: Why Long Context Costs More
sections.content: You just saw one word compare itself against seven others. Attention does that for every token against every other token — so the work grows quadratically. Doubling the context roughly quadruples the attention computation, which is why long-context requests cost more and why models can get less precise in the middle of very long inputs.

sections.heading: Dense vs Mixture-of-Experts
sections.content: A dense model activates every parameter for every token. A Mixture of Experts (MoE) model stores many specialized 'expert' blocks and routes each token through only a few of them — so a model can have trillions of parameters while only using a fraction per token. This is how Kimi K3 ships 2.8 trillion parameters at a workable serving cost. Route some tokens yourself:

visual.caption: Total parameters ≠ active parameters — check both in model specs

sections.heading: What This Explains
sections.content: Three behaviors you can now account for:
bullets: Why generation is word-by-word: each new token requires a full pass through every layer
Why long documents cost more and degrade retrieval quality — attention's quadratic cost
Why 'trillions of parameters' headlines need the active-parameter number next to them

advancedLessons.keyTakeaway: A transformer is an embedding step plus a tall stack of attention-and-transform layers. Attention is pairwise context-gathering — powerful, but its cost grows quadratically with context length.

advancedLessons.title: The Training Pipeline
advancedLessons.subtitle: From raw internet text to a helpful assistant — in three stages.

sections.content: A frontier model is not trained in one step. It goes through a pipeline where each stage has a different goal, different data, and wildly different cost. Knowing the stages lets you decode phrases in model announcements like 'post-trained for agentic tasks' — and understand where model behavior actually comes from.

sections.heading: The Three Stages
sections.content: Every major model follows some version of this pipeline: pre-training on trillions of tokens, supervised fine-tuning on curated examples, then preference training (RLHF). The best way to feel the difference is to ask the same model the same question at each stage:

visual.caption: Capability comes from stage 1 — personality and safety mostly from stages 2-3

sections.heading: Where the Behavior Comes From
sections.content: This division of labor explains a lot. Pre-training gives the model its knowledge and its flaws (training-data bias, cutoff dates). Fine-tuning teaches the chat format. Preference training — RLHF — is where refusals, hedging, tone, and sycophancy get dialed in. When two models built on similar data feel completely different to talk to, you're mostly feeling different preference training, not different intelligence.
bullets: Knowledge and hallucination tendencies → pre-training
Answer format and instruction-following → fine-tuning
Refusals, tone, agreeableness → preference training

sections.heading: Synthetic Data & Distillation
sections.content: Labs increasingly generate training data with AI itself: a strong model produces worked solutions that are filtered — kept only if the code runs or the math checks out — then used to train the next model. Distillation is the targeted version: a large 'teacher' model generates data to train a small 'student,' which is how sub-$1 models got near-frontier quality in 2025-2026. Done with filtering, this works; done indiscriminately and recursively, it degrades models (the 'model collapse' result). The difference is curation, not the synthetic data itself.

sections.heading: The Cost Ladder
sections.content: Rough orders of magnitude, which explain who can play at each level:

elements: Fine-tune a small open model: hundreds of dollars
Frontier pre-training run: tens to hundreds of millions
visual.caption: Compute cost is why open-weight releases from funded labs matter so much

advancedLessons.keyTakeaway: Pre-training builds capability; post-training shapes behavior. When you evaluate a model's 'personality' or safety, you are evaluating choices made in preference training — by people.

advancedLessons.title: Reasoning & Test-Time Compute
advancedLessons.subtitle: Why modern models "think" before answering — and when that helps.

sections.content: Around 2024, progress shifted from making models bigger to letting them think longer. Instead of answering immediately, reasoning models generate internal work first — exploring approaches, catching their own errors — and only then write the reply. This 'test-time compute' is the single biggest change in how frontier AI works since this app's fundamentals course was written.

sections.heading: Two Budgets, Not One
sections.content: A model's quality used to be fixed at training time. Now there are two dials: what was learned during training, and how much compute is spent on your specific question. The same model with a larger thinking budget solves measurably harder problems — which is why 2026 flagships expose effort controls, like the five-level toggle on Claude Opus 5. Try the dial yourself:

visual.caption: Same weights, different answer-time budget — accuracy climbs, then flattens while cost keeps rising

sections.heading: Where Thinking Pays Off
sections.content: The gains are large exactly where single-pass models were weakest:
bullets: Math and formal logic — models reached IMO gold-medal level in 2025
Multi-file coding tasks and debugging
Planning problems with constraints and tradeoffs
NOT: casual writing, summaries, simple facts — there it mostly adds cost and latency

sections.heading: Two Honest Caveats
sections.content: First: the 'thought process' apps display is a cleaned-up summary, not a faithful transcript — research shows the visible reasoning doesn't always match what drove the answer. Second: thinking raises the ceiling on hard problems but does not install a fact-checker. A model can reason for thousands of tokens and still build carefully on a hallucinated premise. Verify conclusions, not effort.

advancedLessons.keyTakeaway: Test-time compute made 'how long should the model think?' a setting you control and pay for. Use it for math, code, and planning; skip it for lookups — and never mistake visible effort for verified truth.

advancedLessons.title: Agents, Tools & MCP
advancedLessons.subtitle: What happens when a model can act, not just answer.

sections.content: An agent is a model in a loop: read the situation, choose an action, observe the result, repeat until the goal is met. The 'actions' are tool calls — run code, search the web, click a button, edit a file. This loop is behind coding agents, computer-use assistants, and most of what 2026 marketing calls 'agentic AI.' Watch one work:

visual.caption: The agent loop — the model never leaves this think → act → observe cycle

sections.heading: MCP: The Universal Adapter
sections.content: Until recently, every tool integration was custom-built. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 and since adopted across the industry, standardizes how models discover and call tools — one protocol connects a model to databases, browsers, calendars, codebases. This is why agent capabilities expanded so fast: the ecosystem stopped rebuilding plumbing and started sharing it.

sections.heading: Why Agents Fail Differently
sections.content: A chatbot mistake produces one wrong paragraph. An agent mistake compounds:
bullets: Errors stack across steps — a misread file in step 2 corrupts every step after it
Confident goal misinterpretation: the agent optimizes for what it thought you meant
Prompt injection: instructions hidden in a webpage or document can hijack the loop from inside
Over-permission: the July 2026 $HOME deletion incident happened with sandbox and approvals disabled

sections.heading: The Safety Playbook
sections.content: The working rules that came out of the 2026 incidents are simple: least privilege (give the agent only the access the task needs), approval gates on destructive actions, sandboxes on by default, and backups that the agent cannot touch. 'Fully autonomous' is a risk setting, not a feature tier.

sections.heading: The Harness Is Not the Model
sections.content: The model generates outputs; the harness supplies instructions, tools, context and permissions. Cursor Agent, Claude Code, Codex, Aider, Cline and OpenHands offer different workflows around models. Some explicitly support local providers, including Cline, Aider and Codex CLI. Check the provider documentation for your product: API compatibility alone does not guarantee that a local server will work.

sources.title: Cursor Agent — tools and model orchestration
Codex CLI reference — local providers and permissions
Cline — local models with Ollama and LM Studio
OpenHands — Agent Canvas and MIT license

advancedLessons.keyTakeaway: Agents are models in an act-observe loop, standardized by MCP. The harness is the loop and the tools; the model is only the brain. Their power and their risk come from the same place — every tool they can use is a tool they can misuse, so scope access like it matters.

advancedLessons.title: Benchmarks & How to Read Model Claims
advancedLessons.subtitle: The skeptic's toolkit for "our new model beats everything."

sections.content: Every model release arrives with a chart where the new model wins. Sometimes it's real progress; sometimes it's chart engineering. This lesson is the applied version of everything in this course: how to read an AI capability claim like a fact-checker.

sections.heading: How Benchmarks Break
sections.content: Four failure modes account for most misleading scores:
bullets: Contamination: test questions leaked into training data — the model memorized, not solved (the documented CursorBench 3.2 case)
Saturation: when every frontier model scores 90%+, the benchmark stops discriminating
Selection: releases cite the benchmarks they win and omit the ones they lose
Setup gaming: best-of-N sampling, special prompting, or extra compute reported as if standard

sections.heading: Try It: The Launch-Day Chart
sections.content: And then there's the oldest trick of all — one that isn't even about the benchmark. Here's a chart pattern you will recognize from real model launches. Look at it, form an impression, then press the button:

visual.caption: Every time you see a bar chart in a model announcement, find the y-axis first.

sections.heading: The Questions That Cut Through
sections.content: When you see "X beats Y," ask:

elements: Who ran the evaluation — the vendor or an independent party?
Is the benchmark public (contaminable) or held-out?
What was the compute setup — one attempt or best of many?
How big is the gap — 0.5% is noise, not news
Does it show up in benchmarks the vendor did not choose?
visual.caption: Five questions that deflate most misleading charts

sections.heading: What Actually Predicts Usefulness
sections.content: Benchmark scores correlate with capability, but the correlation weakens exactly where marketing is strongest — at the frontier, between close competitors. Better signals: independent leaderboards with held-out tasks, head-to-head blind preference rankings, and above all, performance on your task. That's why this app's Compare section shows multiple dimensions instead of one number, and why every model page lists limitations next to capabilities.

advancedLessons.keyTakeaway: A benchmark score is a measurement of one thing under one setup — never 'how good the model is.' The five questions (who ran it, held-out?, what setup, gap size, cherry-picked?) will serve you longer than any leaderboard.

advancedLessons.title: AI Security: Jailbreaks & Prompt Injection
advancedLessons.subtitle: The two attacks that matter — and why one is much harder to fix.

sections.content: As AI moved from chat windows into email clients, browsers, and codebases, it acquired a security problem. Two attack families dominate, they're constantly confused with each other, and the distinction determines what can actually be defended.

sections.heading: Jailbreak vs Prompt Injection
sections.content: A jailbreak is the user attacking the model — crafting prompts (roleplay framing, encoding tricks, many-shot examples) to get around safety training. Prompt injection is a third party attacking the user through the model: malicious instructions hidden in content the AI processes — a webpage, an email, a PDF, a calendar invite — that the model then follows as if they came from you.

elements: Jailbreak: user vs model — user wants the restricted output
Injection: attacker vs user — the model is the weapon, you are the target
visual.caption: Different attacker, different victim, different defenses

sections.heading: Why Injection Is the Hard One
sections.content: Jailbreaks are an arms race the defenders are slowly winning — safety classifiers like those on Claude Fable 5 add a screening layer independent of the model. Injection is structurally harder: transformers have no built-in separation between 'instructions to follow' and 'content to read.' Both arrive as tokens in the same context window. Run the attack yourself — then run it again with a defense on:

visual.caption: Indirect prompt injection — no hacking of the model required, and the fix is permissions, not intelligence

sections.heading: The Defense Stack
sections.content: No single fix exists; real defenses layer:
bullets: Input/output classifiers screening for attack patterns
Privilege separation: content-reading agents should not hold send/delete/pay permissions
Human approval gates on consequential actions
Treating every external document an agent reads as untrusted input

advancedLessons.keyTakeaway: Jailbreaks target the model; injections target you through the model. Injection is unsolved at the architecture level — which is why an agent's permissions matter more than its intelligence.

advancedLessons.title: Open Weights & Running Models Yourself
advancedLessons.subtitle: The other half of the AI world — licenses, quantization, and local AI.

sections.content: Half the models in this app's catalog can be downloaded and run on your own hardware. That half — DeepSeek, Kimi, Muse, Mistral, Command — works on different economics and different rules than the closed APIs, and 2025-2026 made it competitive at the frontier for the first time.

sections.heading: 'Open' Comes in Degrees
sections.content: Precision matters here, because 'open source AI' is used loosely:
bullets: Open weights: the trained parameters are downloadable — but check the license (Kimi K3 requires attribution above 100M monthly users; resellers need agreements)
Open source (strict): weights, training code, and data recipe all published — rare at the frontier
Open API only: you can call it, but nothing is downloadable (GPT-5.6, Claude, Gemini)

sections.heading: Quantization: The Enabler
sections.content: Model weights are stored as high-precision numbers. Quantization rounds them to lower precision — 8-bit, 4-bit, even lower — shrinking memory needs by 2-4x with a small quality cost. It's the reason a model that nominally needs 140GB can run on a 48GB machine, and the reason local AI is practical at all. Squeeze a 70B model yourself and watch what happens:

visual.caption: The 4-bit sweet spot is what local tools like Ollama actually run

sections.heading: The Three-Layer Local Stack
sections.content: Once the weights are on disk you still need software to run them. These are not competing models — they are layers:
bullets: Engine: llama.cpp runs supported GGUF models on CPU and GPU backends and includes a configurable server.
Runtime: Ollama provides model management, a CLI and an API (default port 11434). LM Studio offers desktop and headless operation with an API (default port 1234), using llama.cpp or Apple MLX.
Tools: Cline, Aider and Codex CLI document local-model workflows. LM Studio can also use MCP tools in chat; tool access and network use depend on configuration.

sources.title: llama.cpp — GGUF inference and hardware backends
Ollama — local privacy, cloud and concurrency
LM Studio — supported engines and platforms
LM Studio — headless service and llmster
Cline — local models with Ollama and LM Studio
Codex CLI reference — local providers and permissions
LM Studio — MCP tools in chat

sections.heading: Why This Half Matters
sections.content: Open weights are the reason API prices keep falling (closed labs price against free alternatives), the reason researchers can study how models work internally, and the reason AI capability can't be fully centralized or fully recalled. They're also the reason watermarking and content-policy enforcement have limits — an open model runs wherever someone has the hardware. Every debate about AI control eventually runs through this fact.

advancedLessons.keyTakeaway: Open weights changed AI's power structure: frontier-adjacent capability now runs on hardware you can own, under licenses you should actually read. Quantization is what makes it fit. The runtime (LM Studio, Ollama) loads the file; a harness is what lets that local model act.

benchmarks.name: MMLU
benchmarks.shortDescription: Massive Multitask Language Understanding (57 subjects).
benchmarks.details: A 57-subject multiple-choice test spanning STEM, humanities, social sciences, and professional exams (law, medicine, accounting). Measures broad knowledge and reasoning. Score is overall accuracy across roughly 14,000 questions. Largely saturated by frontier models, which is why MMLU-Pro was created as a successor.

benchmarks.name: MMLU-Pro
benchmarks.shortDescription: Harder, reasoning-heavy successor to MMLU.
benchmarks.details: A more challenging successor to MMLU with 10 answer choices instead of 4 and questions filtered to require multi-step reasoning rather than memorization. About 12,000 questions across 14 subjects. Standard frontier-model headline benchmark.

benchmarks.name: AGIEval
benchmarks.shortDescription: Human standardized exams (SAT, LSAT, civil service, gaokao).
benchmarks.details: Curated questions drawn from human standardized exams — SAT, GRE, LSAT, US civil-service tests, and the Chinese gaokao — used to compare LLMs against actual human exam-takers across reasoning-heavy domains.

benchmarks.name: GPQA
benchmarks.shortDescription: Graduate-level science questions designed to be Google-proof.
benchmarks.details: Hard multiple-choice questions in physics, chemistry, and biology written by domain experts and verified to be unanswerable by web search. Tests deep scientific reasoning without retrieval shortcuts.

benchmarks.name: GPQA Diamond
benchmarks.shortDescription: The hardest 198-question subset of GPQA.
benchmarks.details: The most difficult subset of GPQA: 198 questions where roughly two-thirds of expert PhDs in the relevant field still get them wrong without tools. The standard frontier-model benchmark for graduate-level scientific reasoning.

benchmarks.name: AIME
benchmarks.shortDescription: Elite high-school competition math (15 problems, 3 hours).
benchmarks.details: The American Invitational Mathematics Examination — a 15-problem, 3-hour competition for the top US high-school math students. Each answer is an integer from 0–999. Used as an LLM benchmark because it requires multi-step proof-style problem solving.

benchmarks.name: AIME 2024
benchmarks.shortDescription: AIME I + II 2024 (30 problems total).
benchmarks.details: The AIME I and II competitions held in 2024, totaling 30 problems. A common math-reasoning benchmark for LLMs because it postdates many models’ training cutoffs and is hard to memorize.

benchmarks.name: AIME 2025
benchmarks.shortDescription: AIME I + II 2025 (30 problems total).
benchmarks.details: The 2025 American Invitational Mathematics Examination, used as a fresh, contamination-free reasoning benchmark for the latest frontier models.

benchmarks.name: MATH
benchmarks.shortDescription: Competition-style math problems with worked solutions.
benchmarks.details: 12,500 problems from US high-school math competitions (AMC 10/12, AIME, etc.) graded 1–5 by difficulty, with full worked-out solutions. Tests symbolic and step-by-step reasoning.

benchmarks.name: GSM8K
benchmarks.shortDescription: Grade-school math word problems (2–8 reasoning steps).
benchmarks.details: 8,500 grade-school-level math word problems requiring 2–8 reasoning steps. Now considered saturated by frontier models, but still a useful sanity check and historically important.

benchmarks.name: BBH
benchmarks.shortDescription: BIG-Bench Hard — 23 tasks where pre-2022 LLMs failed.
benchmarks.details: A 23-task subset of BIG-Bench specifically chosen because earlier LLMs failed on them. Tests multi-step logical, causal, and structured reasoning.

benchmarks.name: ARC-AGI
benchmarks.shortDescription: Visual abstraction & reasoning corpus (Chollet).
benchmarks.details: A grid-based visual reasoning challenge designed by François Chollet to test abstraction and skill acquisition rather than memorization. Each task gives a few input/output examples; the model must infer the rule and apply it to a new input. The basis of the ARC Prize. Successors ARC-AGI-2 (harder static tasks) and ARC-AGI-3 (interactive game environments) keep the frontier unsaturated — in July 2026, GPT-5.6 Sol became the first model to beat a public ARC-AGI-3 game.

benchmarks.name: Humanity's Last Exam
benchmarks.shortDescription: Expert-written questions at the frontier of human knowledge.
benchmarks.details: Thousands of questions written by subject-matter experts across dozens of fields, designed to be the hardest broad academic benchmark available — questions that even domain PhDs find difficult. Created as a successor to saturated benchmarks like MMLU. Frontier models still score well below expert-human level, making it a common headline number for new releases.

benchmarks.name: HumanEval
benchmarks.shortDescription: Hand-written Python coding problems with unit tests.
benchmarks.details: 164 hand-written Python programming problems with unit tests. Score is pass@1 (whether the first generated solution passes all tests). Largely saturated by modern frontier models but historically important.

benchmarks.name: MBPP
benchmarks.shortDescription: Mostly Basic Python Problems (~1K crowdsourced tasks).
benchmarks.details: About 1,000 crowdsourced entry-level Python problems with three test cases each. Tests basic code generation against a natural-language problem description.

benchmarks.name: SWE-Bench
benchmarks.shortDescription: Real GitHub issues from popular Python repos.
benchmarks.details: 2,294 real-world software-engineering tasks pulled from GitHub issues across 12 popular Python repositories. The model must produce a patch that resolves the issue and passes the original test suite — much harder than function-level coding because it requires navigating real codebases.

benchmarks.name: SWE-Bench Verified
benchmarks.shortDescription: Human-validated 500-problem subset of SWE-Bench.
benchmarks.details: A 500-problem subset of SWE-Bench where every task was human-reviewed to confirm it is solvable and fairly scored, removing broken or underspecified issues from the original set. The most commonly cited SWE-Bench variant for headline coding-agent numbers.

benchmarks.name: SWE-Bench Pro
benchmarks.shortDescription: Harder, contamination-resistant successor to SWE-Bench.
benchmarks.details: A harder, contamination-resistant successor to SWE-Bench using more diverse codebases (including non-Python and proprietary repos). Often cited as the headline benchmark for autonomous coding agents.

benchmarks.name: Terminal-Bench
benchmarks.shortDescription: Real command-line tasks executed in a live terminal.
benchmarks.details: Evaluates AI agents on realistic tasks carried out in a live terminal environment — compiling code, wrangling data, administering systems, and debugging — scored by whether the end state is correct. Because tasks execute in a real sandbox, it is harder to game than static Q&A benchmarks. Version 2.x is the standard agentic-coding headline number in 2026; Grok 4.5 posted 83.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 at launch.

benchmarks.name: CursorBench
benchmarks.shortDescription: Agentic coding evaluated in real IDE-style sessions.
benchmarks.details: Measures how well a model completes end-to-end coding tasks in realistic editor/agent sessions, weighing both task success and cost per task. Widely cited in 2026 frontier releases: Claude Opus 5 landed within 0.5% of Fable 5’s peak at half the per-task cost. Also a cautionary tale — SpaceXAI disclosed that a Cursor codebase snapshot contaminated Grok 4.5’s training and inflated its score.

benchmarks.name: Frontier-Bench
benchmarks.shortDescription: Cross-domain evaluation suite for 2026 frontier models.
benchmarks.details: A 2026 evaluation suite designed to separate frontier models on hard, cross-domain professional work after older benchmarks saturated. Scores both accuracy and cost per task. Claude Opus 5 led all models on v0.1 at release, more than doubling Opus 4.8’s score at lower cost per task.

benchmarks.name: LiveBench
benchmarks.shortDescription: Frequently-refreshed contamination-free benchmark.
benchmarks.details: A multi-domain benchmark whose questions are continuously refreshed (math, reasoning, coding, language, instruction-following, data analysis) to avoid training-set contamination. Each model is scored against the latest version of the test set.

benchmarks.name: OSWorld
benchmarks.shortDescription: Real desktop tasks across Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS.
benchmarks.details: 369 real-world computer-use tasks (file management, web browsing, multi-app workflows) executable in a real OS environment. Tests whether an agent can drive a desktop with mouse, keyboard, and the file system. The "average human" baseline is roughly 72%.

benchmarks.name: TAU-Bench
benchmarks.shortDescription: Multi-turn tool-use evaluation (retail, airline).
benchmarks.details: Evaluates how well an agent can complete realistic multi-turn tasks (retail customer service, airline bookings) using a defined toolset under strict policy compliance. Tests both action accuracy and conversational dynamics.

benchmarks.name: BFCL
benchmarks.shortDescription: Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard.
benchmarks.details: Evaluates whether a model can correctly call APIs given a natural-language request and an OpenAPI-style spec. Covers simple, multiple, parallel, and nested tool-call scenarios.

benchmarks.name: Frontend Code Arena
benchmarks.shortDescription: Head-to-head human voting on generated frontend UIs.
benchmarks.details: A live arena where models generate working frontend interfaces from the same prompt and humans vote on the better result, producing Elo-style rankings. Because judging rendered UIs is hard to game with memorization, it became a closely watched coding leaderboard in 2026 — Kimi K3 debuted at #1, above Claude Fable 5.

benchmarks.name: MCP Atlas
benchmarks.shortDescription: Tool-use evaluation across real MCP servers.
benchmarks.details: Evaluates agents on multi-step tasks that require discovering and correctly using tools exposed over the Model Context Protocol (MCP) — the open standard for connecting AI models to external services. Tests tool discovery, argument construction, and multi-server orchestration. Meta claimed the #1 spot with Muse Spark 1.1 in July 2026.

benchmarks.name: MMMU
benchmarks.shortDescription: College-level multimodal questions across 30 subjects.
benchmarks.details: 11,500 college-level multimodal questions (charts, figures, schematics, diagrams) spanning 30 academic subjects. The standard headline benchmark for visual reasoning.

benchmarks.name: MMVet
benchmarks.shortDescription: 6-capability vision-language evaluation.
benchmarks.details: Evaluates vision-language models across 6 core capabilities (recognition, OCR, knowledge, language generation, spatial awareness, math) requiring integrated reasoning over images and text.

benchmarks.name: MathVista
benchmarks.shortDescription: Visual math reasoning across diagrams and figures.
benchmarks.details: About 6,000 visual math questions covering diagrams, plots, scientific figures, and geometric drawings. Tests integrated visual + symbolic reasoning end-to-end.

benchmarks.name: ChartQA
benchmarks.shortDescription: Question answering over charts and graphs.
benchmarks.details: About 32,000 human-authored questions about real charts and graphs, requiring visual reasoning and arithmetic over the rendered figure (not just OCR).

benchmarks.name: DocVQA
benchmarks.shortDescription: Document visual question answering.
benchmarks.details: 50,000 questions over 12,767 document images (forms, receipts, letters). Tests OCR + layout understanding + reasoning together.

benchmarks.name: Chatbot Arena
benchmarks.shortDescription: Crowdsourced blind side-by-side preference voting.
benchmarks.details: A live leaderboard where users blind-compare two anonymous model responses to the same prompt and vote for the better one. Computes Elo-style ratings from millions of head-to-head matchups. Maintained by LMSYS.

benchmarks.name: MT-Bench
benchmarks.shortDescription: Multi-turn instruction-following judged by GPT-4.
benchmarks.details: 80 multi-turn conversation prompts across 8 categories, judged by GPT-4 on a 1–10 scale. A quick proxy for conversational quality, though limited by judge bias.

benchmarks.name: IFEval
benchmarks.shortDescription: Verifiable instruction-following.
benchmarks.details: About 500 prompts with verifiable instructions (e.g. "respond in exactly 3 bullet points", "include the word ‘apple’ twice"). Scored deterministically without an LLM judge.

benchmarks.name: HellaSwag
benchmarks.shortDescription: Adversarial sentence-completion commonsense reasoning.
benchmarks.details: Adversarially-filtered sentence-completion benchmark for commonsense reasoning. Mostly saturated by modern models but historically important and still cited.

benchmarks.name: WinoGrande
benchmarks.shortDescription: Pronoun-resolution commonsense reasoning at scale.
benchmarks.details: 44,000 Winograd-schema-style commonsense pronoun-resolution problems, scaled and adversarially filtered. Largely saturated.

benchmarks.name: TruthfulQA
benchmarks.shortDescription: Resistance to common misconceptions and falsehoods.
benchmarks.details: 817 questions across 38 categories targeting common human misconceptions (e.g. health myths, urban legends). Tests whether the model echoes popular falsehoods or gives the truthful answer.
